title: Connecting my illumos box to a Japanese ISP
content_html:
I moved an Ethernet cable from my router to an OmniOS box that I call fridge. The other end was connected to the modem provided for my Docomo Hikari line. This was meant to be the last test of a Rust networking project I had worked on during weekends since the end of March. I had written a daemon that could manage a native DS-Lite tunnel on Linux and illumos. If it went well, the box would connect directly to the ISP and provide IPv4 connectivity through that tunnel.

The modem lights looked normal. OmniOS received router advertisements and installed a default IPv6 route on ixgbe1. It did not, however, receive an address that could be used to reach the Internet.

$ ipadm show-addr
ADDROBJ           TYPE     STATE        ADDR
lo0/v4            static   ok           127.0.0.1/8
ixgbe1/v6         addrconf ok           fe80::ae1f:6bff:fe6c:5ca7%ixgbe1/10

$ netstat -nr -f inet6
Destination/Mask            Gateway                   Flags  If
default                     fe80::be4a:56ff:fe1c:3c10 UG     ixgbe1

There was a route, but only a link local address to use as its source. Restarting the modem and recreating the IPv6 interface changed nothing. Four months earlier I would probably have assumed that the tunnel was the missing part. By this point I had also implemented the provisioning protocol used by my ISP, an SMF service, and an OmniOS package. The cable test exposed a more basic gap.

I started the project because I wanted to learn more about the illumos network stack. I had also been looking for a Rust project that would let me work directly with operating system interfaces. An article by Ryan Goodfellow about the life of an IPv6 address on illumos had stayed in my mind. It follows one address through ipadm, libraries, doors, STREAMS, and the kernel. I wanted a problem that would make me visit some of the same layers.

There was also a practical goal. fridge already runs services on my home network. If it could terminate the ISP connection as well, I could use it as the entry point to that network.

Calling it my ISP connection hides some Japanese telecom layering. The physical access runs over NTT's FLET'S network. My retail contract for that line is Docomo Hikari, while ASAHI Net provides Internet connectivity on top of it using native IPv6 over IPoE and IPv4 over DS-Lite. All three names therefore describe parts of the same connection, but they do not play the same role.

DS-Lite exists because an ISP can provide native IPv6 without assigning a public IPv4 address to every customer. The customer side component is called a B4. It takes an IPv4 packet and places it inside an IPv6 packet addressed to an ISP endpoint called the AFTR. The AFTR removes the outer packet and performs IPv4 network address translation before sending the traffic to the Internet. RFC 6333 describes the architecture.

Applications on the customer network still see ordinary IPv4. Their packets reach the B4, which uses the reserved 192.0.0.0/29 range for the point to point side of the tunnel. The outer IPv6 packet travels over the access network to the AFTR. Replies follow the same path in reverse. Once the tunnel exists, the daemon is no longer involved in moving each packet. Encapsulation and forwarding remain inside the operating system network stack.

The B4 does not need to implement packet forwarding itself. Both Linux and illumos already know how to create an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel. The first useful experiment was therefore small. I created an iptun link on OmniOS, configured a matching Linux host on the same network as a temporary AFTR, assigned the reserved DS-Lite IPv4 endpoints, and installed a route. IPv4 pings crossed the tunnel in both directions.

That result seemed to remove the largest risk because the kernel data path worked. The remaining task looked like turning a few administrative commands into a daemon that could discover the two IPv6 endpoints and keep the tunnel in the desired state. I treated the tunnel as the uncertain part and ISP provisioning as information that some existing service would eventually hand to it. Building the tunnel daemon followed that plan, while finding a reliable source for the ISP information became the rest of the project.

I did not want the program to run dladm, ipadm, and route as subprocesses. Calling the underlying interfaces would teach me more, avoid parsing command output, and make it possible to observe and reconcile state through the same APIs. The Linux backend used netlink. The illumos backend used libdladm to create the tunnel link, libipadm to create its IP interface, socket ioctls to configure its addresses, and a PF_ROUTE socket for the IPv4 default route.

This choice made the Rust side more interesting than a sequence of command invocations. Some illumos interfaces are regular C library calls, while others exchange structures whose layout comes directly from system headers. Each foreign call required deciding which values could be represented safely in Rust, how long pointers remained valid, and which resources needed cleanup after a partial failure. The daemon runs as root, so an incorrect structure was not just an inconvenient type error. It could ask the kernel to change the wrong network state.

The division between libipadm and the direct ioctls was not part of the original design. It came from the debugging detour in the project.

Four bytes between two processes

The 64 bit Rust daemon could create an iptun link and plumb its IP interface, but assigning the point to point IPv4 address failed with IPADM_NOTSUP. The equivalent ipadm create-addr command worked. After the failed call, the interface remained present without an address because libipadm had rolled back the kernel change.

I started by tracing system and library calls with truss, followed the error through the illumos source, and then used DTrace to narrow it to an nvlist_unpack call inside ipmgmtd. The packed nvlist looked valid in the client, although the service read it four bytes later than I expected.

At first I suspected that I had translated one of the C structures incorrectly. That would have been a familiar FFI mistake, but comparing the buffers did not support it. The client passed an nvlist beginning with a valid encoding header, while the service saw four zero bytes before that header. The data itself had survived the door call, but the two processes disagreed about where it began.

The clue that changed the investigation was easy to overlook. After looking at the service with mdb, searching the Internet, and asking an LLM for help, I finally noticed 32 bit register names such as %ebp rather than %rbp. The Rust program was a 64 bit process using /lib/amd64/libipadm.so.1, while /lib/inet/ipmgmtd was a 32 bit process. They communicate through an illumos door, a local procedure call mechanism.

One of the private door request structures contains a size_t field followed by the nvlist. Its layout depends on the architecture.

32 bit ipmgmtd             64 bit libipadm caller

0   command                0   command
4   flags                  4   flags
8   nvlist size, 4 bytes   8   nvlist size, 8 bytes
12  nvlist                 16  nvlist

The service expected the nvlist at offset 12, while the client placed it at offset 16. As a result, the first four bytes passed to the unpacker came from the upper half of the size field. The unpacker rejected them, ipmgmtd returned an error, and libipadm translated it to status 36.

The failure only appeared in my process because the shipped ipadm command is also 32 bit. Its structure matches the 32 bit service, so the same private protocol works when used by the system tool. A 64 bit C program would have encountered the same problem. With that knowledge, I found illumos issue 17851, which already described the same ipadm_create_addr() failure and proposed replacing size_t with a fixed width uint32_t. The source even contains a comment saying that door structures must have the same size on amd64 and i386. This particular structure does not follow that rule.

I kept the working parts of libipadm, but bypassed address creation with the same SIOCSLIFADDR family of ioctls used below the library. The tunnel became functional, although ipadm show-addr displays the address as dslite0/? because it was not registered with ipmgmtd. Later I found that Oxide's netadm-sys had dealt with the same boundary by defining the door field with a fixed width. I may eventually follow the same path to restore the missing ipadm object registration.

Another part of the daemon needed the local IPv6 address that the kernel would use to reach the AFTR. On Linux, ip route get returns a preferred source address, and my first implementation read the corresponding netlink attribute. illumos also has a route lookup through PF_ROUTE, so I expected to write a second version of the same idea. For the address field, however, the kernel selects the first logical IP interface on the link. On a normal IPv6 interface that is the link local address, not necessarily the source chosen for a remote destination. route -nv get confirmed the source code on the running system.

The replacement was a connected UDP socket. Binding it to the unspecified IPv6 address and connecting it to the AFTR makes the kernel perform its usual route and source selection. UDP connect() does not need to send a packet. getsockname() then returns the selected local address. The same three standard socket calls worked on both systems, so I deleted the tested Linux netlink implementation.

By July the daemon could create, inspect, update, and remove the tunnel. Creating it once was different from running it as a service. The local IPv6 endpoint could disappear or change when the upstream address changed. The remote endpoint came from DNS or provisioning and had its own refresh lifecycle. A crash could leave behind some combination of the tunnel link, IP interface, address, and route. Running a fixed sequence of setup commands at startup would either destroy working state or fail when the system no longer matched the expected order.

I built the daemon around a reconcile loop instead. On every wake it recalculated the desired endpoints, inspected the actual kernel state, and selected the smallest action needed to make them agree. It could keep a correct tunnel, bring up one that was down, update properties that could change in place, or rebuild it when the endpoints changed. Linux netlink and illumos PF_ROUTE events only woke the loop. They were hints that something might have changed, while the kernel remained the source of truth. This also allowed a restarted daemon to adopt an existing tunnel without interrupting traffic.

Where the AFTR came from

None of that answered one remaining question. How would it learn the address of the real AFTR?

RFC 6334 defines DHCPv6 option 64 for this purpose. The option contains an AFTR name that the B4 resolves through DNS. I originally considered adding a small DHCPv6 client to the daemon, but a host already has a client bound to UDP port 546. Two clients cannot safely divide ownership of leases and replies on that port. It made more sense to let the system client keep that responsibility and pass the result to dslite-b4 through its set-aftr command.

Well, that simple boundary became less portable each time I tested it. ISC dhclient can request option 64 and run an exit hook with the result. systemd-networkd can request the option but does not make the returned AFTR name available to another program. NetworkManager can expose received options and notify a dispatcher, but its configuration does not add option 64 to the request list. On illumos I could define option 64 in inittab6, the system's DHCP option table, so that dhcpagent could request and decode it. It did not, however, provide a dependable notification when the value changed and could restore a stale value after a later reply omitted it. These experiments did not prove that RFC 6334 was unusable everywhere. They showed that decoding a DHCP option is only one part of an integration. The client also has to request it, expose it, and report its removal.

For better or worse, my access line did not return option 64 anyway. ASAHI Net's DS-Lite service, called v6connect, uses a Japanese provisioning protocol called HB46PP. A client first asks its DNS resolver for a TXT record at 4over6.info. On the provider network, that name returns the URL and trust mode of a provisioning service. An HTTPS request then returns the available IPv4 over IPv6 mechanism and its endpoint.

The DNS part is intentional. The same name can return different provisioning information depending on the access network from which it is queried. That lets a common client discover the service selected for its line without shipping a list of Japanese providers. It also means that native IPv6 and the correct resolver must already work before HB46PP can discover anything.

I implemented HB46PP as a separate Rust crate because the protocol can provision mechanisms other than DS-Lite. Implementing it involved more than parsing DNS and JSON. The client had to apply the trust mode from the DNS bootstrap, handle redirects without leaking provisioning tokens to another origin, and follow refresh deadlines and retry instructions. From behind my existing router it discovered dslite.v6connect.net, and the daemon created a tunnel to the resolved AFTR. The daemon status and a kernel route lookup then showed the expected path:

$ dslite-b4 status
Desired: resolved
AFTR: dslite.v6connect.net (hb46pp)
Local IPv6: [redacted]
Remote IPv6: 2001:c28:1:301::11
Last action: create

$ ipadm show-addr | grep dslite0
dslite0/?         static   ok           192.0.0.2->192.0.0.1

$ route -n get 1.1.1.1
   route to: 1.1.1.1
destination: default
       mask: default
    gateway: 192.0.0.1
  interface: dslite0
      flags: <UP,GATEWAY,DONE,STATIC>

At that stage my own router was still between fridge and the bridged ISP modem, providing IPv6 and DNS. That was enough to test the tunnel, but not the whole path from the modem. The final direct connection test would show whether stock illumos could obtain IPv6 and DNS on this access line.

What the ISP delegated

This brings the story back to ixgbe1 and its link local address. A packet capture showed router advertisements with the Managed and Other Configuration flags, but no global prefix that the host could use for address autoconfiguration. dhcpagent responded by sending a DHCPv6 Solicit containing IA_NA, which requests one non temporary address. No Advertise or Reply arrived.

I first wondered whether the ISP had remembered the router's MAC address, or whether I had left part of the illumos interface configuration behind. The packet capture kept showing the same unanswered request after the modem restart and interface rebuild, ruling out the simpler versions of those explanations.

The ISP had previously delegated a /56 to my router. ISC DHCP is no longer maintained, which made it suitable for an experiment but not a permanent answer:

$ dhclient -6 -P --prefix-len-hint 56 ixgbe1

dhclient  -> Solicit   IA_PD /56
ISP       <- Advertise IA_PD /56
dhclient  -> Request   IA_PD /56
ISP       <- Reply     IA_PD /56

The server answered immediately with a delegated /56 and normal lease lifetimes. I appreciate that model because it lets me divide the allocation among my own networks. IA_PD, however, delegates a routed prefix rather than configuring an address on ixgbe1. The client must decide how to use the prefix, advertise its subnets, and maintain the lease. illumos dhcpagent could request a host address through IA_NA, but it was not prepared to take on that router role.

For the experiment I selected one /128 from the delegated prefix and added it temporarily to ixgbe1. IPv6 pings and HTTPS requests then worked, which confirmed that the prefix was routed to the host.

The DHCP Reply also included the addresses of two DNS resolvers for the access network. Once I configured one address from the delegated prefix and those resolvers, HB46PP found the AFTR and the daemon brought up dslite0. IPv4 ICMP and HTTPS worked through the native illumos tunnel with my router no longer in the path. This confirmed that both HB46PP and the tunnel implementation worked against the real service.

What I had configured by hand was now the missing part. Making it permanent would require a DHCPv6 client that acquired, renewed, and rebound the delegation, divided the prefix among local networks, configured addresses and DNS, and withdrew that configuration when the lease expired. Because it would have to coexist with or replace dhcpagent, this was another system network service rather than a small adapter around dslite-b4.

Earlier in the project I had decided that the daemon should not become a second DHCP client. That decision still seems right. Owning the B4 tunnel is a narrow responsibility. Competing with the operating system client on port 546, while each process believes it controls addresses and DNS, would leave neither process with a reliable view of the lease. The alternative would be a new component that replaces the relevant part of dhcpagent, which is another project rather than the final milestone of this one.

The repository now contains the result of that work, including Linux and illumos backends, a reconcile loop, and service definitions. I also published two Rust crates, dslite-b4 and hb46pp. The daemon can manage DS-Lite when the host already has working IPv6 provisioning. It cannot turn stock illumos into a direct router for this Asahi Net line.

I had wanted the project to end with fridge at the edge of my home network. Instead, it ended at a boundary in the network stack that I do not yet want the daemon to cross. For now that feels like a reasonable place to stop, write down what I learned, and think about what a future project would need to own.

What I had configured by hand was now the missing part. Making it permanent would require a DHCPv6 client that acquired, renewed, and rebound the delegation, divided the prefix among local networks, configured addresses and DNS, and withdrew that configuration when the lease expired. Because it would have to coexist with or replace dhcpagent, this was another system network service rather than a small adapter around dslite-b4. Earlier in the project I had decided that the daemon should not become a second DHCP client. That decision still seems right. Owning the B4 tunnel is a narrow responsibility. Competing with the operating system client on port 546, while each process believes it controls addresses and DNS, would leave neither process with a reliable view of the lease. The alternative would be a new component that replaces the relevant part of dhcpagent, which is another project rather than the final milestone of this one. The repository now contains the result of that work, including Linux and illumos backends, a reconcile loop, and service definitions. I also published two Rust crates, dslite-b4 and hb46pp. The daemon can manage DS-Lite when the host already has working IPv6 provisioning. It cannot turn stock illumos into a direct router for this Asahi Net line. I had wanted the project to end with fridge at the edge of my home network. Instead, it ended at a boundary in the network stack that I do not yet want the daemon to cross. For now that feels like a reasonable place to stop, write down what I learned, and think about what a future project would need to own.

blocks.html_en: DS-Lite exists because an ISP can provide native IPv6 without assigning a public IPv4 address to every customer. The customer side component is called a B4. It takes an IPv4 packet and places it inside an IPv6 packet addressed to an ISP endpoint called the AFTR. The AFTR removes the outer packet and performs IPv4 network address translation before sending the traffic to the Internet. RFC 6333 describes the architecture.

sentences.en: DS-Lite exists because an ISP can provide native IPv6 without assigning a public IPv4 address to every customer.
sentences.zh: DS-Lite 的存在是因为 ISP 可以提供本机 IPv6，而无需为每个客户分配公共 IPv4 地址。

sentences.en: The customer side component is called a B4.
sentences.zh: 客户端组件称为 B4。

sentences.en: It takes an IPv4 packet and places it inside an IPv6 packet addressed to an ISP endpoint called the AFTR.
sentences.zh: 它获取 IPv4 数据包并将其放入寻址到称为 AFTR 的 ISP 端点的 IPv6 数据包中。

sentences.en: The AFTR removes the outer packet and performs IPv4 network address translation before sending the traffic to the Internet.
sentences.zh: AFTR 在将流量发送到 Internet 之前删除外部数据包并执行 IPv4 网络地址转换。

sentences.en: RFC 6333 describes the architecture.
sentences.zh: RFC 6333 描述了该架构。

blocks.html_en: Applications on the customer network still see ordinary IPv4. Their packets reach the B4, which uses the reserved 192.0.0.0/29 range for the point to point side of the tunnel. The outer IPv6 packet travels over the access network to the AFTR. Replies follow the same path in reverse. Once the tunnel exists, the daemon is no longer involved in moving each packet. Encapsulation and forwarding remain inside the operating system network stack.

The data itself had survived the door call, but the two processes disagreed about where it began.

sentences.zh: Rust 程序是使用 /lib/amd64/libipadm.so.1 的 64 位进程，而 /lib/inet/ipmgmtd 是 32 位进程。

blocks.html_en: One of the private door request structures contains a size_t field followed by the nvlist. Its layout depends on the architecture.

sentences.en: One of the private door request structures contains a size_t field followed by the nvlist.

sentences.en: The unpacker rejected them, ipmgmtd returned an error, and libipadm translated it to status 36.

blocks.html_en: I built the daemon around a reconcile loop instead. On every wake it recalculated the desired endpoints, inspected the actual kernel state, and selected the smallest action needed to make them agree. It could keep a correct tunnel, bring up one that was down, update properties that could change in place, or rebuild it when the endpoints changed. Linux netlink and illumos PF_ROUTE events only woke the loop. They were hints that something might have changed, while the kernel remained the source of truth. This also allowed a restarted daemon to adopt an existing tunnel without interrupting traffic.

blocks.html_en: RFC 6334 defines DHCPv6 option 64 for this purpose. The option contains an AFTR name that the B4 resolves through DNS. I originally considered adding a small DHCPv6 client to the daemon, but a host already has a client bound to UDP port 546. Two clients cannot safely divide ownership of leases and replies on that port. It made more sense to let the system client keep that responsibility and pass the result to dslite-b4 through its set-aftr command.

sentences.zh: 该选项包含 B4 通过 DNS 解析的 AFTR 名称。

sentences.zh: 两个客户端无法安全地分割该端口上的租约和回复的所有权。

sentences.en: It made more sense to let the system client keep that responsibility and pass the result to dslite-b4 through its set-aftr command.

blocks.html_en: Well, that simple boundary became less portable each time I tested it. ISC dhclient can request option 64 and run an exit hook with the result. systemd-networkd can request the option but does not make the returned AFTR name available to another program. NetworkManager can expose received options and notify a dispatcher, but its configuration does not add option 64 to the request list. On illumos I could define option 64 in inittab6, the system's DHCP option table, so that dhcpagent could request and decode it. It did not, however, provide a dependable notification when the value changed and could restore a stale value after a later reply omitted it. These experiments did not prove that RFC 6334 was unusable everywhere. They showed that decoding a DHCP option is only one part of an integration. The client also has to request it, expose it, and report its removal.

sentences.en: Well, that simple boundary became less portable each time I tested it.
sentences.zh: 好吧，每次我测试这个简单的边界时，它的可移植性就变得越来越差。

sentences.en: ISC dhclient can request option 64 and run an exit hook with the result.
sentences.zh: ISC dhclient 可以请求选项 64 并使用结果运行退出挂钩。

sentences.zh: systemd-networkd 可以请求该选项，但不会使返回的 AFTR 名称可供其他程序使用。

sentences.zh: NetworkManager 可以公开接收到的选项并通知调度程序，但其配置不会将选项 64 添加到请求列表中。

sentences.en: On illumos I could define option 64 in inittab6, the system's DHCP option table, so that dhcpagent could request and decode it.
sentences.zh: 在 illumos 上，我可以在 inittab6（系统的 DHCP 选项表）中定义选项 64，以便 dhcpagent 可以请求并解码它。

sentences.en: It did not, however, provide a dependable notification when the value changed and could restore a stale value after a later reply omitted it.
sentences.zh: 然而，当值发生变化时，它没有提供可靠的通知，并且可以在稍后的回复忽略它后恢复陈旧的值。

sentences.en: These experiments did not prove that RFC 6334 was unusable everywhere.
sentences.zh: 这些实验并没有证明 RFC 6334 在任何地方都无法使用。

sentences.en: They showed that decoding a DHCP option is only one part of an integration.
sentences.zh: 他们表明，解码 DHCP 选项只是集成的一部分。

blocks.html_en: For better or worse, my access line did not return option 64 anyway. ASAHI Net's DS-Lite service, called v6connect, uses a Japanese provisioning protocol called HB46PP. A client first asks its DNS resolver for a TXT record at 4over6.info. On the provider network, that name returns the URL and trust mode of a provisioning service. An HTTPS request then returns the available IPv4 over IPv6 mechanism and its endpoint.

sentences.en: For better or worse, my access line did not return option 64 anyway.
sentences.zh: 无论好坏，我的接入线无论如何都没有返回选项 64。

sentences.en: ASAHI Net's DS-Lite service, called v6connect, uses a Japanese provisioning protocol called HB46PP.
sentences.zh: ASAHI Net 的 DS-Lite 服务称为 v6connect，使用称为 HB46PP 的日本配置协议。

sentences.en: A client first asks its DNS resolver for a TXT record at 4over6.info.
sentences.zh: 客户端首先向其 DNS 解析器请求 4over6.info 上的 TXT 记录。

That lets a common client discover the service selected for its line without shipping a list of Japanese providers. It also means that native IPv6 and the correct resolver must already work before HB46PP can discover anything.

sentences.en: That lets a common client discover the service selected for its line without shipping a list of Japanese providers.

blocks.html_en: Earlier in the project I had decided that the daemon should not become a second DHCP client. That decision still seems right. Owning the B4 tunnel is a narrow responsibility. Competing with the operating system client on port 546, while each process believes it controls addresses and DNS, would leave neither process with a reliable view of the lease. The alternative would be a new component that replaces the relevant part of dhcpagent, which is another project rather than the final milestone of this one.

content_html_zh:
我将一根以太网线从路由器移到了一个我称之为冰箱的 OmniOS 盒子上。 另一端连接到为我的 Docomo Hikari 线路提供的调制解调器。 这是我自 3 月底以来在周末进行的 Rust 网络项目的最后一次测试。 我编写了一个守护进程，可以管理 Linux 和 illumos 上的本机 DS-Lite 隧道。 如果进展顺利，盒子将直接连接到 ISP 并通过该隧道提供 IPv4 连接。

调制解调器指示灯看起来正常。 OmniOS 收到路由器通告并在 ixgbe1 上安装默认 IPv6 路由。 然而，它没有收到可用于访问互联网的地址。

$ ipadm show-addr
ADDROBJ           TYPE     STATE        ADDR
lo0/v4            static   ok           127.0.0.1/8
ixgbe1/v6         addrconf ok           fe80::ae1f:6bff:fe6c:5ca7%ixgbe1/10

$ netstat -nr -f inet6
Destination/Mask            Gateway                   Flags  If
default                     fe80::be4a:56ff:fe1c:3c10 UG     ixgbe1

有一条路由，但只有一个链接本地地址用作其源。 重新启动调制解调器并重新创建 IPv6 接口没有任何改变。 四个月前，我可能会认为隧道就是缺失的部分。 此时，我还实现了 ISP 使用的配置协议、SMF 服务和 OmniOS 软件包。 电缆测试暴露了一个更基本的差距。

我启动这个项目是因为我想了解有关 illumos 网络堆栈的更多信息。 我还一直在寻找一个 Rust 项目，它可以让我直接使用操作系统界面。 Ryan Goodfellow 在 illumos 上发表的一篇关于 IPv6 地址生命周期的文章一直留在我的脑海中。 它遵循一个地址通过 ipadm、库、门、STREAMS 和内核。 我想要一个能让我访问某些相同层的问题。

还有一个实际的目标。 冰箱已经在我的家庭网络上运行服务。 如果它也可以终止 ISP 连接，我可以将其用作该网络的入口点。

将其称为我的 ISP 连接隐藏了一些日本电信分层。 物理访问通过 NTT 的 FLET'S 网络运行。 我对该系列产品的零售合同是 Docomo Hikari，而 ASAHI Net 使用本机 IPv6 over IPoE 和 IPv4 over DS-Lite 在此基础上提供互联网连接。 因此，这三个名称都描述了同一连接的各个部分，但它们并不发挥相同的作用。

DS-Lite 的存在是因为 ISP 可以提供本机 IPv6，而无需为每个客户分配公共 IPv4 地址。 客户端组件称为 B4。 它获取 IPv4 数据包并将其放入寻址到称为 AFTR 的 ISP 端点的 IPv6 数据包中。 AFTR 在将流量发送到 Internet 之前删除外部数据包并执行 IPv4 网络地址转换。 RFC 6333 描述了该架构。

客户网络上的应用程序仍然看到普通的 IPv4。 它们的数据包到达 B4，B4 使用隧道点对点侧保留的 192.0.0.0/29 范围。 外部 IPv6 数据包通过接入网络传输到 AFTR。 回复遵循相同的相反路径。 一旦隧道存在，守护进程就不再参与移动每个数据包。 封装和转发保留在操作系统网络堆栈内部。

B4本身不需要实现报文转发。 Linux 和 illumos 都已经知道如何创建 IPv4-in-IPv6 隧道。 因此，第一个有用的实验规模很小。 我在 OmniOS 上创建了一个 iptun 链接，在同一网络上配置了一个匹配的 Linux 主机作为临时 AFTR，分配了保留的 DS-Lite IPv4 端点，并安装了路由。 IPv4 ping 双向穿越隧道。

这个结果似乎消除了最大的风险，因为内核数据路径有效。 剩下的任务看起来像是将一些管理命令转变为一个守护进程，该守护进程可以发现两个 IPv6 端点并将隧道保持在所需的状态。 我将隧道视为不确定的部分，并将 ISP 配置视为某些现有服务最终会交给它的信息。 按照该计划构建隧道守护进程，而为 ISP 信息寻找可靠的来源则成为项目的其余部分。

我不希望程序将 dladm、ipadm 和路由作为子进程运行。 调用底层接口可以教会我更多知识，避免解析命令输出，并可以通过相同的 API 观察和协调状态。 Linux后端使用netlink。 illumos 后端使用 libdladm 创建隧道链接，使用 libipadm 创建其 IP 接口，使用套接字 ioctl 来配置其地址，以及用于 IPv4 默认路由的 PF_ROUTE 套接字。

这种选择使 Rust 方面比一系列命令调用更有趣。 一些 illumos 接口是常规 C 库调用，而其他接口则交换其布局直接来自系统头文件的结构。 每个外部调用都需要决定哪些值可以在 Rust 中安全地表示、指针保持有效多长时间以及部分失败后需要清理哪些资源。 该守护进程以 root 身份运行，因此不正确的结构不仅仅是一个不方便的类型错误。 它可能会要求内核更改错误的网络状态。

libipadm 和直接 ioctl 之间的划分并不是原始设计的一部分。 来源于项目中的调试弯路。

两个进程之间的四个字节

64 位 Rust 守护进程可以创建 iptun 链接并检测其 IP 接口，但分配点对点 IPv4 地址失败并出现 IPADM_NOTSUP。 等效的 ipadm create-addr 命令有效。 调用失败后，接口仍然存在，但没有地址，因为 libipadm 已回滚内核更改。

我首先使用 truss 跟踪系统和库调用，通过 illumos 源跟踪错误，然后使用 DTrace 将其范围缩小到 ipmgmtd 内的 nvlist_unpack 调用。 打包的 nvlist 在客户端中看起来有效，尽管服务读取它的时间比我预期晚了四个字节。

起初我怀疑我错误地翻译了其中一个 C 结构。 这是 FFI 常见的错误，但比较缓冲区并不支持这一点。 客户端传递了一个以有效编码标头开头的 nvlist，而服务在该标头之前看到了四个零字节。 数据本身在上门呼叫中幸存下来，但两个进程对于数据的开始位置存在分歧。

改变调查的线索很容易被忽视。 在使用 mdb 查看服务、搜索互联网并向 LLM 寻求帮助后，我终于注意到 32 位寄存器名称，例如 %ebp 而不是 %rbp。 Rust 程序是使用 /lib/amd64/libipadm.so.1 的 64 位进程，而 /lib/inet/ipmgmtd 是 32 位进程。 它们通过 illumos 门（一种本地过程调用机制）进行通信。

私家门请求结构之一包含 size_t 字段，后跟 nvlist。 它的布局取决于架构。

32 bit ipmgmtd             64 bit libipadm caller

0   command                0   command
4   flags                  4   flags
8   nvlist size, 4 bytes   8   nvlist size, 8 bytes
12  nvlist                 16  nvlist

服务期望 nvlist 位于偏移量 12 处，而客户端将其放置在偏移量 16 处。 结果，传递给解包器的前四个字节来自大小字段的上半部分。 解包器拒绝它们，ipmgmtd 返回错误，libipadm 将其转换为状态 36。

该故障仅出现在我的进程中，因为附带的 ipadm 命令也是 32 位的。 它的结构与32位服务相匹配，因此当系统工具使用时，相同的私有协议可以工作。 64 位 C 程序也会遇到同样的问题。 有了这些知识，我发现了 illumos 问题 17851，它已经描述了相同的 ipadm_create_addr() 失败，并建议用固定宽度的 uint32_t 替换 size_t。 该消息来源甚至包含一条评论，称 amd64 和 i386 上的门结构必须具有相同的大小。 这个特定的结构不遵循该规则。

我保留了 libipadm 的工作部分，但使用库下面使用的相同 SIOCSLIFADDR 系列 ioctl 绕过了地址创建。 尽管 ipadm show-addr 将地址显示为 dslite0/?，但隧道已恢复正常工作。 因为它没有向 ipmgmtd 注册。 后来我发现Oxide的netadm-sys通过定义固定宽度的门字段来处理相同的边界。 我最终可能会遵循相同的路径来恢复丢失的 ipadm 对象注册。

守护程序的另一部分需要内核用来访问 AFTR 的本地 IPv6 地址。 在 Linux 上，iproute get 返回首选源地址，我的第一个实现读取相应的 netlink 属性。 illumos 还通过 PF_ROUTE 进行路由查找，因此我希望编写相同想法的第二个版本。 然而，对于地址字段，内核选择链路上的第一个逻辑 IP 接口。 在普通 IPv6 接口上，它是链路本地地址，不一定是为远程目标选择的源。 route -nv 获取正在运行的系统上确认的源代码。

替代方案是连接的 UDP 套接字。 将其绑定到未指定的 IPv6 地址并将其连接到 AFTR 使内核执行其通常的路由和源选择。 UDP connect()不需要发送数据包。 getsockname() 然后返回选定的本地地址。 相同的三个标准套接字调用在两个系统上都有效，因此我删除了经过测试的 Linux netlink 实现。

到 7 月，守护进程可以创建、检查、更新和删除隧道。 创建一次与将其作为服务运行不同。 当上游地址更改时，本地 IPv6 端点可能会消失或更改。 远程端点来自 DNS 或配置，并且有自己的刷新生命周期。 崩溃可能会留下隧道链路、IP 接口、地址和路由的某些组合。 在启动时运行固定序列的设置命令会破坏工作状态，或者当系统不再与预期顺序匹配时失败。

我围绕协调循环构建了守护进程。 每次唤醒时，它都会重新计算所需的端点，检查实际的内核状态，并选择使它们达成一致所需的最小操作。 它可以保持正确的隧道，恢复已关闭的隧道，更新可能发生变化的属性，或者在端点发生变化时重建它。 Linux netlink 和 illumos PF_ROUTE 事件仅唤醒循环。 它们暗示某些事情可能已经改变，而内核仍然是真相的来源。 这还允许重新启动的守护进程采用现有隧道而不中断流量。

AFTR 从何而来

这些都没有回答剩下的问题。 它如何得知真实 AFTR 的地址？

为此，RFC 6334 定义了 DHCPv6 选项 64。 该选项包含 B4 通过 DNS 解析的 AFTR 名称。 我最初考虑向守护进程添加一个小型 DHCPv6 客户端，但主机已经有一个绑定到 UDP 端口 546 的客户端。 两个客户端无法安全地分割该端口上的租约和回复的所有权。 让系统客户端承担该责任并通过其 set-aftr 命令将结果传递给 dslite-b4 更有意义。

好吧，每次我测试这个简单的边界时，它的可移植性就变得越来越差。 ISC dhclient 可以请求选项 64 并使用结果运行退出挂钩。 systemd-networkd 可以请求该选项，但不会使返回的 AFTR 名称可供其他程序使用。 NetworkManager 可以公开接收到的选项并通知调度程序，但其配置不会将选项 64 添加到请求列表中。 在 illumos 上，我可以在 inittab6（系统的 DHCP 选项表）中定义选项 64，以便 dhcpagent 可以请求并解码它。 然而，当值发生变化时，它没有提供可靠的通知，并且可以在稍后的回复忽略它后恢复陈旧的值。 这些实验并没有证明 RFC 6334 在任何地方都无法使用。 他们表明，解码 DHCP 选项只是集成的一部分。 客户端还必须请求它、公开它并报告它的删除。

无论好坏，我的接入线无论如何都没有返回选项 64。 ASAHI Net 的 DS-Lite 服务称为 v6connect，使用称为 HB46PP 的日本配置协议。 客户端首先向其 DNS 解析器请求 4over6.info 上的 TXT 记录。 在提供商网络上，该名称返回配置服务的 URL 和信任模式。 然后，HTTPS 请求返回可用的 IPv4 over IPv6 机制及其端点。

DNS 部分是有意为之的。 相同的名称可以返回不同的配置信息，具体取决于查询它的接入网络。 这使得普通客户可以发现为其产品线选择的服务，而无需提供日本提供商的列表。 这也意味着本机 IPv6 和正确的解析器必须已经工作，HB46PP 才能发现任何内容。

我将 HB46PP 实现为单独的 Rust 箱，因为该协议可以提供 DS-Lite 以外的机制。 实现它不仅仅涉及解析 DNS 和 JSON。 客户端必须从 DNS 引导程序应用信任模式，处理重定向而不将配置令牌泄漏到另一个源，并遵循刷新截止日期和重试指令。 它从我现有的路由器后面发现了 dslite.v6connect.net，并且守护进程创建了一条通往已解析 AFTR 的隧道。 然后，守护进程状态和内核路由查找显示了预期的路径：

$ dslite-b4 status
Desired: resolved
AFTR: dslite.v6connect.net (hb46pp)
Local IPv6: [redacted]
Remote IPv6: 2001:c28:1:301::11
Last action: create

$ ipadm show-addr | grep dslite0
dslite0/?         static   ok           192.0.0.2->192.0.0.1

$ route -n get 1.1.1.1
   route to: 1.1.1.1
destination: default
       mask: default
    gateway: 192.0.0.1
  interface: dslite0
      flags: <UP,GATEWAY,DONE,STATIC>

在那个阶段，我自己的路由器仍然位于冰箱和桥接的 ISP 调制解调器之间，提供 IPv6 和 DNS。 这足以测试隧道，但不足以测试来自调制解调器的整个路径。 最终的直连测试将显示库存 illumos 是否可以在此接入线路上获取 IPv6 和 DNS。

ISP 委托的内容

这让故事回到了 ixgbe1 及其链接本地地址。 数据包捕获显示带有托管和其他配置标志的路由器通告，但没有主机可用于地址自动配置的全局前缀。 dhcpagent 通过发送包含 IA_NA 的 DHCPv6 Solicit 进行响应，该请求请求一个非临时地址。 没有收到广告或回复。

我首先想知道 ISP 是否记住了路由器的 MAC 地址，或者我是否留下了部分 illumos 接口配置。 在调制解调器重新启动和接口重建后，数据包捕获继续显示相同的未应答请求，排除了这些解释的简单版本。

ISP 之前已将 /56 委托给我的路由器。 这表明有不同的 DHCPv6 请求。 illumos dhcpagent 不实现前缀委派，因此我在 OmniOS 上的临时目录中构建了 ISC DHCP 4.4.3-P1。 ISC DHCP 不再维护，这使得它适合实验，但不是永久的答案：

$ dhclient -6 -P --prefix-len-hint 56 ixgbe1

dhclient  -> Solicit   IA_PD /56
ISP       <- Advertise IA_PD /56
dhclient  -> Request   IA_PD /56
ISP       <- Reply     IA_PD /56

服务器立即以委派的 /56 和正常的租约寿命进行响应。 DS-Lite 本身不需要前缀委派，但此访问服务期望连接的路由器请求一个。 我很欣赏这个模型，因为它让我可以在自己的网络之间分配分配。 然而，IA_PD 委托路由前缀而不是在 ixgbe1 上配置地址。 客户端必须决定如何使用前缀、通告其子网以及维护租约。 illumos dhcpagent 可以通过 IA_NA 请求主机地址，但它不准备承担该路由器角色。

在实验中，我从委托前缀中选择了一个 /128 并将其临时添加到 ixgbe1。 然后 IPv6 ping 和 HTTPS 请求起作用，确认前缀已路由到主机。

DHCP 回复还包括接入网络的两个 DNS 解析器的地址。 一旦我从委托前缀和这些解析器配置了一个地址，HB46PP 就会找到 AFTR，并且守护进程会启动 dslite0。 IPv4 ICMP 和 HTTPS 通过本机 illumos 隧道工作，而我的路由器不再位于路径中。 这证实了 HB46PP 和隧道实现都对真实服务起作用。

我手动配置的现在是缺失的部分。 使其永久化需要 DHCPv6 客户端获取、更新和反弹委派，在本地网络、配置的地址和 DNS 之间划分前缀，并在租约到期时撤回该配置。 因为它必须与 dhcpagent 共存或取代 dhcpagent，所以这是另一个系统网络服务，而不是 dslite-b4 周围的小型适配器。

在项目的早期，我决定守护进程不应成为第二个 DHCP 客户端。 这个决定看起来仍然是正确的。 拥有 B4 隧道是一项狭隘的责任。 在端口 546 上与操作系统客户端竞争，虽然每个进程都认为自己控制着地址和 DNS，但两个进程都无法获得可靠的租约视图。 另一种选择是用一个新组件来取代 dhcpagent 的相关部分，这是另一个项目，而不是该项目的最终里程碑。

该存储库现在包含该工作的结果，包括 Linux 和 illumos 后端、协调循环和服务定义。 我还发布了两个 Rust 包，dslite-b4 和 hb46pp。 当主机已经具有有效的 IPv6 配置时，守护程序可以管理 DS-Lite。 它无法将库存 illumos 转变为该 Asahi Net 线路的直接路由器。

我本来希望该项目以家庭网络边缘的冰箱结束。 相反，它结束于网络堆栈中的一个边界，我还不希望守护进程跨越该边界。 现在感觉这是一个合理的地方，可以停下来，写下我学到的东西，并思考未来的项目需要拥有什么。
